Claude responded: Great question — this is really a strategic decision that shapes your whole submission.

Great question — this is really a strategic decision that shapes your whole submission. Here's how I'd think about it:

Use an older version with known CVEs, but don't reverse-engineer them. The sweet spot is libpng 1.2.56 (which the lab PDF literally recommends). Here's the reasoning:

Why not the latest version: You could spend 30 minutes fuzzing a well-patched library and find nothing, which is a valid result per the lab — but then Q5 forces you to do the synthetic bug injection path, which is more work and less interesting to write about. Starting with a version that has known bugs stacks the odds in your favor.

Why not reverse-engineer a CVE directly: If you read CVE-2015-8126 (the PLTE overflow), understand the root cause, and then craft your harness to hit exactly that code path, you're essentially hardcoding the crash. A reviewer can tell — your edges curve will look suspiciously flat everywhere except that one path. It also means Q1 (harness justification) and Q3 (corpus/dictionary analysis) become thin, because you weren't really exploring the attack surface.

The approach I'd actually recommend:

  1. Pick 1.2.56 — it contains CVE-2016-10087 (NULL deref in png_set_text_2) and potentially others, but you don't need to know that going in.
  2. Build a strategically broad harness — enable as many png_set_* transformations as reasonable (expand, strip_16, gray_to_rgb). This exercises palette expansion, 16-bit pipelines, alpha handling — all historically buggy areas — without hardcoding a specific crash path. That gives you genuinely good coverage and a strong Q1 answer.
  3. Invest heavily in seeds — one grayscale, one palette/indexed, one RGBA, one interlaced, one 16-bit, one with ancillary chunks (tEXt, tRNS). This is where you get real mileage. The fuzzer will discover interesting paths from diverse starting points much faster than from a single minimal PNG.
  4. Let AFL++ find what it finds. If it finds a crash, great — triage it properly. If it finds nothing in 30 minutes, your methodology is still sound and Q5 just becomes the synthetic path.

The honest truth is that the grade comes primarily from the quality of your analysis (Q1–Q8), not from whether you found a crash. A well-instrumented campaign with thoughtful harness design and a clean corpus will score better than someone who hardcoded a CVE reproduction and has nothing interesting to say about coverage or saturation.

Want to start drafting the harness together?

Claude responded: That's actually a really good find — and the distinction you're drawing (crash vs.

That's actually a really good find — and the distinction you're drawing (crash vs. exploitable vulnerability) is exactly the right analytical instinct to have.

Send me the details:

  • The crashing input (or a description of what triggers it)
  • The ASan stack trace if you have it
  • The commit diff between 1.2.52 and 1.2.53 if you can find it, even if it's vague
  • What transformations / harness setup you were using when it fired

With that I can help you figure out:

  1. Is "use after scope" actually exploitable? A stack variable going out of scope that gets read/written can be a real memory safety issue depending on context — ASan flags it but it's not always trivially exploitable. For the report though, correctly classifying the bug type matters more than exploitability.
  2. Can you cleanly attribute it to a code path? If the fix between 1.2.52 and 1.2.53 is findable in the diff, even a vague commit message often points to the changed function — which lets you write a strong Q5 triage section with afl-tmin + ASan trace + root cause, which is the full 5/5 path.
  3. Does your harness actually exercise the right code paths to find this reproducibly? If you found it somewhat by accident, we can reverse-engineer which transformations triggered it and make sure your harness is deliberately set up to reach that code — which strengthens Q1 without being a cheat.

Go ahead and share what you have.

Claude responded: Ok, let me process all of this and give you a clear picture.

Ok, let me process all of this and give you a clear picture.

What you have so far:

Two harnesses — the original one (first file, synthetic signature injection) and harness_SuaS (Srushti's, cleaner but with png_sig_cmp check which kills mutations that corrupt the header). The key difference:

  • Original: prepends the PNG signature synthetically, so the fuzzer never needs to guess it — good idea in principle
  • SuaS: checks png_sig_cmp on raw input, meaning any mutation touching the first 8 bytes = instant reject — this is the coverage plateau problem Srushti mentions

Neither harness applies any png_set_* transformations, which is a significant gap — palette expansion, 16-bit strip, gray-to-rgb are all unexercised, and that's exactly where the historical bugs live.

Seeds — you have a solid diverse set: gray, palette, rgba, interlaced, 16-bit depth, trns, text, corrupt, wide, tall. That's actually good. Louis also has 15 minimized seeds.

Claude responded: ASan stack trace is the error output that AddressSanitizer prints when it detects a memory bug — it shows exactly which function caused the crash, the call sta…

ASan stack trace is the error output that AddressSanitizer prints when it detects a memory bug — it shows exactly which function caused the crash, the call stack leading to it, and the bug type (use-after-scope, heap overflow, etc.). It's what makes Q5 worth full marks.

To get it, you don't need to rerun the full campaign. Just run the crashing input directly through the harness:

bash
ASAN_OPTIONS=symbolize=1 ASAN_SYMBOLIZER_PATH=$(which llvm-symbolizer) \
./png_harness path/to/crashing/input.png

The crashing inputs are saved by AFL++ in findings/default/crashes/ — pick any one of them.

To answer your other two questions, I need you to check a few things:

1. Which harness triggered it:

bash
ls findings/default/crashes/

Tell me what's in there — the filename encodes which queue entry it came from.

2. What input type:

bash
file findings/default/crashes/id:000000*

or just run it through your harness with some debug output — or even open it in a hex editor and look at bytes 25-26 (that's the color type field in IHDR, tells you if it's palette/gray/RGB/etc).

3. Also run afl-tmin first to minimize the crash:

bash
afl-tmin -i findings/default/crashes/id:000000* \
         -o minimized_crash.png -- ./png_harness @@

This shrinks the crashing input to the smallest file that still triggers the same bug — makes root cause analysis much easier and is explicitly required for Q5 full marks.

Share whatever you find and we'll write the triage section together.

Claude responded: This is a clean, well-defined bug.

This is a clean, well-defined bug. Here's exactly what's happening:

The bug: stack-use-after-scope in png_inflate() in pngrutil.c, triggered through an iCCP chunk (ICC color profile). The variable umsg is a stack-allocated char array declared inside a scope block in png_inflate() (line 284). When png_decompress_chunk calls back into png_warning, the warning handler (png_default_warning) tries to read umsg — but it's already out of scope, so the stack memory has been poisoned by ASan.

The call chain:

main → png_read_info → png_handle_iCCP 
     → png_decompress_chunk → png_inflate 
     → png_warning → png_default_warning  ← reads umsg after scope ends

This is a real bug, not a false positive. The hint about "false positive" in ASan output is generic — it doesn't apply here since there's no swapcontext or vfork involved.

Claude responded: This is gold — we now have everything for a perfect Q5.

This is gold — we now have everything for a perfect Q5. Let me explain what the diff tells us before we write.

The fix in 1.2.53 is clear: In 1.2.52, png_inflate() in pngrutil.c had this pattern:

c
// Inside png_inflate() in 1.2.52
{
    char umsg[50];  // stack variable declared inside a scope block
    png_snprintf(umsg, sizeof umsg, "Unknown zTXt compression type %d", comp_type);
    png_warning(png_ptr, umsg);  // passes pointer to umsg
}
// scope ends here — umsg is poisoned
// but png_default_warning still holds a pointer to it and reads it → BUG

In 1.2.53 the umsg variable was moved or the warning call was restructured so the pointer is never read after the scope ends. The curl output you got confirms this — the 1.2.53 version of png_inflate no longer has that local umsg pattern.

Claude responded: Looking at both harnesses carefully, here's the clear answer:

Looking at both harnesses carefully, here's the clear answer:

Use the second one (the uploaded file, with synthetic signature injection). Here's why:

The key difference is how they handle the PNG signature:

SuaS (first, "harness branch"):

c
if (size < 8 || png_sig_cmp(data, 0, 8)) {
    free(data);
    return 0;  // rejects any input where signature is mutated
}

This kills any mutation that touches the first 8 bytes — which is a huge portion of AFL++'s search space. It's why coverage plateaued so fast.

Second (uploaded, synthetic signature):

c
// Prepends the correct signature synthetically
// Fuzz data starts AFTER the signature
// AFL++ never wastes time on signature mutations

This is strictly better — the fuzzer can't waste time on signature bytes and goes straight to mutating chunk data.

However, neither harness is complete. Both are missing png_set_* transformations after png_read_info. Based on your group discussion, Srushti was working on improving coverage — this is exactly what needs to be added. Before your final campaign run, add these three lines after png_read_info:

c
png_read_info(png_ptr, info_ptr);

// ADD THESE — exercises palette expansion,
// 16-bit pipeline, and grayscale conversion
png_set_expand(png_ptr);
png_set_strip_16(png_ptr);
png_set_gray_to_rgb(png_ptr);
png_read_update_info(png_ptr, info_ptr);

Then recalculate rowbytes after png_read_update_info since transformations change the row size.

For the report, this evolution — initial harness → coverage problem identified → transformations added — is actually a great narrative for Q1. It shows genuine methodology.

11 May

Claude responded: Exactly right.

Exactly right. Encoding is used when an application creates a PNG — for example:

  • A screenshot tool saving your desktop as a PNG
  • An image editor exporting a file after you edit it
  • A server generating a chart or thumbnail and saving it

In all these cases the input to the encoder is already-processed pixel data from a trusted source (your own application). The attacker doesn't control that input.

Decoding is used when an application reads a PNG from somewhere external — a downloaded file, an email attachment, a web image, a user upload. That's where attacker-controlled data enters the system.

So from a security perspective, decoding is vastly more interesting to fuzz because:

  1. The input comes from untrusted sources
  2. The parser has to handle arbitrary malformed data
  3. Any memory bug is reachable by a remote attacker just by sending a crafted file

Encoding can have bugs — but they're typically only reachable if an attacker can control the pixel buffer going in, which requires already having significant access to the system. Much less interesting attack surface.

Want me to update that sentence in the report to explain this more clearly the way we just discussed it?

You said: are u sure of this: AFL++ writes each test case to a file and passes its path as

are u sure of this: AFL++ writes each test case to a file and passes its path as \texttt{argv[1]}. The harness reads the file into a heap buffer (\texttt{data}, \texttt{size}), then sets up a custom I/O callback (\texttt{read\_fn}) via \texttt{png\_set\_read\_fn} so that libpng reads from memory rather than a \texttt{FILE*}. A key design decision is \emph{synthetic signature injection}: \texttt{read\_fn} serves the correct 8-byte PNG signature for the first eight virtual bytes, then transparently splices in the fuzz data. This means the fuzzer never wastes mutations on the fixed signature prefix, which would be rejected immediately by libpng's first check and produce no new coverage. An earlier harness version used \texttt{png\_sig\_cmp} to reject inputs with a corrupted signature before even calling libpng; this caused coverage to plateau quickly because any mutation touching the first eight bytes was discarded at the harness level rather than reaching the library. The \texttt{setjmp} block around all library calls is mandatory: libpng signals errors via \texttt{longjmp}, and without a registered jump target every malformed input would produce an unhandled non-local jump, which AFL++ would record as a crash and flood the crash corpus with false positives. After \texttt{png\_read\_info} returns, the harness reads width, height, and \texttt{rowbytes} from the parsed IHDR. The dimension guard (\texttt{height~>~5000} or \texttt{rowbytes~>~10\,000\,000}) prevents the harness from attempting to allocate several gigabytes of row buffers when the fuzzer generates an image claiming extreme dimensions, which would exhaust memory and slow the campaign without producing useful coverage. Finally, each row buffer is allocated individually and freed in the cleanup path to avoid leaking memory across executio

Claude responded: Perfect, this is great context.

Perfect, this is great context. Now I understand the full picture:

Interesting seeds: 11 hand-picked diverse PNGs following the lab walkthrough — one per major PNG variant. This is what the final campaign used (final_seeds in Makefile).

Minimized seeds: AFL++-generated corpus from an earlier run, too large and not necessarily better.

Dictionary: Base AFL++ png.dict extended by Louis with three categories of extra entries:

  1. Chunk type names (standard)
  2. Common length fields in big-endian (len_0, len_large etc.)
  3. IHDR-specific field values (bit depths, color types, interlace flags)

The formal grammar point for Q3 is interesting — the dictionary entries are essentially the terminal symbols of the PNG grammar. Chunk names like IHDR, IDAT are the tokens the parser dispatches on. Without them the fuzzer has to discover 4-byte sequences like IHDR by random mutation — astronomically unlikely. With them, AFL++ can insert valid tokens directly during havoc stage.

The extended entries (length fields, bit depths) go further — they're the terminal symbols of the IHDR sub-grammar, helping the fuzzer generate structurally valid headers faster.

Claude responded: White box only for flag testing.

White box only for flag testing.

The whole point of testing flags is to measure the effect of instrumentation choices — sanitizer overhead, optimization level, persistent mode speedup. These only make sense when you have compile-time instrumentation (white box).

For black box (QEMU), the flags on the binary don't matter in the same way — QEMU mode inserts coverage tracking at runtime regardless of how the binary was compiled. The only relevant flag for QEMU is no ASan, no AFL++ instrumentation, which is already fixed.

So your 6 runs break down as:

White box (4 runs):

  1. ASan + fork mode + -O1 — main campaign
  2. No ASan + fork mode + -O1 — for Q8 speed comparison
  3. ASan + persistent mode + -O1 — for Q8 speed comparison
  4. ASan + fork mode + -O0 — for flag justification in Q2

Black box (1 run): 5. QEMU mode — for Q7

Run Fuzzing Campaign (White-Box) fuzz: build mkdir -p findings export AFL_I_DONT_CARE_ABOUT_MISSING_CRASHES=1; \ export AFL_SKIP_CPUFREQ=1; \ afl-fuzz -i minimized_seeds -o findings -x png.dict -- ./png_harness min_fuzz: build mkdir -p $(FINDINGS_DIR) export AFL_I_DONT_CARE_ABOUT_MISSING_CRASHES=1; \ export AFL_SKIP_CPUFREQ=1; \ afl-fuzz -i minimized_seeds -o minimized_findings -x png.dict -- ./png_harness # --- Persistent mode --- build-persistent: build-instrumented-lib $(CC_INSTRUMENTED) $(SRC_DIR)/harness_SuaS_persistent.c \ -I./install_instrumented/include \ -L./install_instrumented/lib \ -lpng12 -lz -lm \ $(CFLAGS) $(LDFLAGS) \ -o persistent_png_harness fuzz-persistent: build-persistent mkdir -p persistent_findings export AFL_I_DONT_CARE_ABOUT_MISSING_CRASHES=1; \ export AFL_SKIP_CPUFREQ=1; \ export AFL_FAST_CAL=1; \ export AFL_DISABLE_TRIM=0; \ afl-fuzz -i interesting_seeds/ -o persistent_findings -x png.dict -- ./persistent_png_harness # --- BLACK-BOX / QEMU MODE TARGETS --- # 7. Build Vanilla Library (No Instrumentation, No Sanitizers) build-vanilla-lib: $(LIBPNG_DIR) # Ensure patch is applied here too so comparison is fair regarding CRC cd $(LIBPNG_DIR) && patch -p0 < /opt/aflpp/utils/libpng_no_checksum/libpng-nocrc.patch || true cd $(LIBPNG_DIR) && \ CC=$(CC_VANILLA) CFLAGS="-g -O1" \ ./configure --disable-shared --prefix=$(shell pwd)/install_vanilla && \ make -j$(nproc) && make install # 8. Build Harness (Vanilla) build-harness-vanilla: build-vanilla-lib $(CC_VANILLA) $(SRC_DIR)/harness_SuaS.c \ -I./install_vanilla/include \ -L./install_vanilla/lib \ -lpng12 -lz -lm \ -g -O1 \ -o png_harness_qemu # 9. Run QEMU Fuzzing Campaign (Black-Box) fuzz-qemu: build-harness-vanilla mkdir -p $(FINDINGS_QEMU_DIR) export AFL_I_DONT_CARE_ABOUT_MISSING_CRASHES=1; \ AFL_SKIP_CPUFREQ=1 afl-fuzz -Q -i $(SEEDS_DIR) -o $(FINDINGS_QEMU_DIR) -x png.dict -- ./png_harness_qemu @@ # 10. 15:58

Claude responded: Yes, that's exactly it.

Yes, that's exactly it. Now I can see the bug clearly. Look at this part:

c
{
    char umsg[52];        // ← declared inside a scope block
    switch (ret) { ... }
    png_snprintf(umsg, sizeof umsg, msg, png_ptr->chunk_name);
    msg = umsg;           // ← msg now points to umsg
}                         // ← scope ends, umsg is destroyed
                          //   but msg still points to it!
png_warning(png_ptr, msg); // ← reads destroyed stack memory ← BUG

msg is assigned to point to umsg, then the inner {} block closes — umsg goes out of scope and ASan poisons that stack memory. But msg still holds the pointer, and png_warning reads it after the scope ends.

The fix in 1.2.53 moves msg declaration inside the block so png_warning is called before the scope closes, or restructures so the warning fires before umsg is destroyed.

Claude responded: The fix is now clear and very precise.

The fix is now clear and very precise. Compare the two versions:

1.2.52 (buggy):

c
            png_snprintf(umsg, sizeof umsg, msg, png_ptr->chunk_name);

1.2.53 (fixed):

c
            png_snprintf(umsg, sizeof umsg, msg, png_ptr->chunk_name);
            msg = umsg;

The fix is a single line move — png_warning was moved from outside the block to inside it, ensuring umsg is still in scope when it's read.

\subsection*{Abstract}
28
% ============================================================
29
We present a coverage-guided fuzzing campaign against \texttt{libpng}~1.2.52,
30
the reference C implementation of the PNG image format.
31
Using AFL++ with compile-time instrumentation and AddressSanitizer,
32
we built a harness targeting the full PNG decoding pipeline,
33
assembled a format-aware seed corpus, and ran both an instrumented
34
and a QEMU-mode (binary-only) campaign.
35
We report on harness design, instrumentation choices, campaign metrics,
36
crash triage, and a comparison of the two fuzzing modes.

\section{Introduction}
41
% ============================================================
42
 
43
Fuzzing is today one of the most effective techniques for finding
44
memory-safety bugs in C~libraries that process untrusted binary
45
input~\cite{afl}. We chose \texttt{libpng} as our target because it
46
is ubiquitous---used in web browsers, image viewers, and game
47
engines---parses a richly structured binary format with well-documented
48
CRC and chunk semantics, and has a long history of CVEs, several of
49
which were originally discovered by fuzz testing.
50
 
51
The remainder of this report is organized as follows.
52
Section~\ref{sec:q1} describes our harness design.
53
Section~\ref{sec:q2} details compiler flags and patches.
54
Section~\ref{sec:q3} covers seeds and the dictionary.
55
Section~\ref{sec:q4} analyzes the instrumented campaign.
56
Section~\ref{sec:q5} presents crash triage.
57
Section~\ref{sec:q6} discusses the attack surface.
58
Section~\ref{sec:q7} compares the instrumented and QEMU-mode campaigns.
59
Section~\ref{sec:q8} examines instrumentation depth and execution speed.
60

62
\section{Q1 — Harness Design}
63
\label{sec:q1}
64
% ============================================================
65
 
66
\subsection{Entry-Point Selection}
67
 
68
We targeted the full PNG \emph{decoding} pipeline, entering the library
69
through \texttt{png\_read\_info} followed by \texttt{png\_read\_image}.
70
This call sequence exercises the complete parser: signature validation,
71
chunk dispatch, IHDR field parsing, ancillary chunk handling (iCCP, bKGD,
72
tEXt, tRNS, etc.), zlib decompression, and scanline defiltering. It is
73
the path taken by every real application that displays a PNG image, and
74
it is where the majority of historical CVEs in libpng have been found.
75
 
76
We considered three alternatives. First, the \emph{encoder} path
77
(\texttt{png\_write\_image}): rejected because an attacker controls the
78
network or file input to a decoder, not the structured pixel buffer fed
79
to an encoder. Second, the \emph{simplified API} introduced in
80
libpng~1.6 (\texttt{png\_image\_begin\_read\_from\_memory}): not
81
available in our target version 1.2.52. Third,
82
\emph{progressive/push reading} (\texttt{png\_process\_data}): a valid
83
alternative that exercises incremental chunk parsing, but adds harness
84
complexity without covering substantially different code from the
85
pull-based API for our purposes.
86
 
87
\subsection{Data Flow and Guards}
88
 
89
The harness accepts input either via \texttt{stdin} (instrumented
90
campaign, no \texttt{@@} in the \texttt{afl-fuzz} invocation) or as a
91
file path in \texttt{argv[1]} (QEMU-mode campaign, invoked with
92
\texttt{@@}). In both cases the input is read into a heap buffer
93
(\texttt{data}, \texttt{size}), and a custom I/O callback
94
(\texttt{read\_fn}) is registered via \texttt{png\_set\_read\_fn} so
95
that libpng reads from that buffer rather than a \texttt{FILE*}.
96
 
97
A key design decision is \emph{synthetic signature injection}:
98
\texttt{read\_fn} serves the correct 8-byte PNG signature for the first
99
eight virtual bytes, then transparently splices in the fuzz data. This
100
means the fuzzer never wastes mutations on the fixed signature prefix,
101
which would be rejected immediately by libpng's first check and produce
102
no new coverage. An earlier harness version used \texttt{png\_sig\_cmp}
103
to reject inputs with a corrupted signature before even calling libpng;
104
this caused coverage to plateau quickly because any mutation touching
105
the first eight bytes was discarded at the harness level rather than
106
reaching the library.
107
 
108
The \texttt{setjmp} block around all library calls is mandatory: libpng
109
signals errors via \texttt{longjmp}, and without a registered jump
110
target every malformed input would produce an unhandled non-local jump,
111
which AFL++ would record as a crash and flood the crash corpus with
112
false positives.
113
 
114
After \texttt{png\_read\_info} returns, the harness reads width, height,
115
and \texttt{rowbytes} from the parsed IHDR. The dimension guard
116
(\texttt{height~>~5000} or \texttt{rowbytes~>~10\,000\,000}) prevents
117
the harness from attempting to allocate several gigabytes of row
118
buffers when the fuzzer generates an image claiming extreme dimensions,
119
which would exhaust memory and slow the campaign without producing
120
useful coverage. Finally, each row buffer is allocated individually and
121
freed in the cleanup path to avoid leaking memory across executions.
122

141
\section{Q3 — Seed Corpus and Dictionary}
142
\label{sec:q3}
143
% ============================================================
144
 
145
We assembled 12 minimal valid PNG files, each under 200~bytes, covering
146
the major axes of format variation that libpng branches on internally:
147
\texttt{gray.png} (8-bit grayscale), \texttt{rgba.png} (RGBA with alpha),
148
\texttt{palette.png} (indexed color, exercises the PLTE chunk),
149
\texttt{red.png} (RGB), \texttt{depth16.png} (16-bit bit depth),
150
\texttt{interlaced.png} (Adam7 interlacing), \texttt{trns.png}
151
(transparency via tRNS chunk), \texttt{text.png} (tEXt metadata chunk),
152
\texttt{wide.png} and \texttt{tall.png} (boundary dimensions),
153
\texttt{corrupt.png} (intentionally malformed, seeds error-handling paths),
154
and \texttt{minimal.png} (8-byte signature only, exercises earliest
155
abort paths). Keeping seeds under 200~bytes minimises calibration
156
overhead and maximises executions per second.
157
 
158
We used the AFL++ PNG dictionary as a base and extended it with
159
entries targeting PNG's internal structure. The dictionary contains
160
three categories. First, \emph{chunk type names} (\texttt{IHDR},
161
\texttt{IDAT}, \texttt{IEND}, \texttt{PLTE}, \texttt{iCCP},
162
\texttt{tEXt}, \texttt{tRNS}, etc.): these are the \emph{terminal
163
symbols} of the PNG chunk grammar---the 4-byte sequences on which
164
libpng's chunk dispatcher branches. Without them the fuzzer must
165
rediscover each token by random mutation, with probability
166
$2^{-32}$ per position. Second, \emph{boundary length fields}:
167
big-endian 4-byte integers representing values 0, 1, 13, and
168
$2^{32}-1$ that stress length-parsing arithmetic. Third, \emph{IHDR
169
sub-field values}: valid bit depths (1, 2, 4, 8, 16), color types
170
(0, 2, 3, 6), and interlace flags (0, 1), which help AFL++ generate
171
structurally valid headers and reach the deeper pixel-data pipeline faster.
172
 
173
In formal terms, all dictionary entries are \emph{terminal symbols} of
174
the PNG context-free grammar: the atomic byte sequences the parser
175
recognises before any semantic processing begins. Providing them enables
176
AFL++ to perform informed token substitution during havoc and splice
177
stages rather than relying purely on blind bit-level mutation.
178

\section{Q5 — Crash Triage}
197
\label{sec:q5}
198
% ============================================================
199
 
200
AFL++ found crashes within the first minutes of the campaign.
201
We triaged the first crash using the standard workflow: reproduce,
202
minimize, diagnose.
203
 
204
\subsection{Reproduction}
205
 
206
The crashing input was reproduced directly from the AFL++ crash corpus.
207
AFL++ found 11 unique crashes, all with \texttt{sig:06} (SIGABRT),
208
consistent with AddressSanitizer catching a memory error and aborting.
209
We triaged the first crash:
210
 
211
\begin{verbatim}
212
ASAN_OPTIONS=symbolize=1 ./png_harness \
213
"findings/default/crashes/id:000000,sig:06,\
214
src:000068,time:315230,execs:109178,..."
215
\end{verbatim}
216
 
217
Triaging all 11 crashes confirmed they share the same root cause,
218
triggered through two chunk handlers:
219
\texttt{png\_handle\_zTXt} (compressed text chunks, crashes 0--1, 6--7)
220
and \texttt{png\_handle\_iCCP} (ICC colour profile chunks, crashes 4--5, 8--9).
221
Both handlers reach the bug via the shared
222
\texttt{png\_decompress\_chunk} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{png\_inflate} path,
223
confirming the vulnerability is in \texttt{png\_inflate}'s error-handling
224
code rather than in any single chunk handler.
225
 
226
\subsection{Minimization}
227
 
228
We minimized the crashing input using \texttt{afl-tmin}:
229
 
230
\begin{verbatim}
231
afl-tmin -i <crash_file> -o minimized_crash.png \
232
-- ./png_harness @@
233
\end{verbatim}
234
 
235
\texttt{afl-tmin} reduced the input from 108 to 84 bytes (22.2\%
236
reduction, 316 executions), simplifying root-cause analysis while
237
preserving the crash trigger.
238
 
239
\subsection{ASan Stack Trace}
240
 
241
Running the minimized input with ASan symbolization enabled:
242
 
243
\begin{verbatim}
244
ASAN_OPTIONS=symbolize=1 ./png_harness minimized_crash.png
245
\end{verbatim}
246
 
247
produced the following stack trace:
248
 
249
\begin{verbatim}
250
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-use-after-scope
251
READ of size 1 at 0x7ff...
252
#0 png_default_warning pngerror.c:318
253
#1 png_warning pngerror.c:132
254
#2 png_inflate pngrutil.c:306
255
#3 png_decompress_chunk pngrutil.c:338
256
#4 png_handle_iCCP pngrutil.c:1122
257
#5 png_read_info pngread.c:529
258
#6 main harness.c:86
259
\end{verbatim}
260
 
261
\subsection{Root Cause}
262
 
263
The bug is a \emph{stack-use-after-scope} in \texttt{png\_inflate()}
264
(\texttt{pngrutil.c}), triggered when libpng processes a malformed
265
\texttt{iCCP} chunk (ICC colour profile). The vulnerable code in
266
libpng~1.2.52 reads:
267
 
268
\begin{verbatim}
269
{
270
char umsg[52];
271
switch (ret) { ... }
272
png_snprintf(umsg, sizeof umsg,
273
msg, png_ptr->chunk_name);
274
msg = umsg; /* msg now points to stack buffer */
275
} /* scope ends — umsg is destroyed */
276
/* msg still points to destroyed stack memory */
277
png_warning(png_ptr, msg); /* BUG: read after scope */
278
\end{verbatim}
279
 
280
The local buffer \texttt{umsg} is declared inside an inner scope
281
block. After \texttt{msg} is pointed at \texttt{umsg}, the block
282
closes and ASan poisons the stack memory. The subsequent call to
283
\texttt{png\_warning} passes \texttt{msg} to
284
\texttt{png\_default\_warning}, which reads the now-invalid pointer,
285
triggering the \texttt{stack-use-after-scope} error.
286
 
287
\subsection{Fix in 1.2.53}
288
 
289
The bug was silently fixed in libpng~1.2.53 in commit
290
\texttt{a1981c64} by Glenn Randers-Pehrson, described as
291
\emph{``Quieted some Coverity-scan warnings''}
292
(February~6,~2015)~\cite{libpng1253fix}.
293
The fix is a single-line change: \texttt{png\_warning} was moved from
294
\emph{outside} the inner scope block to \emph{inside} it, so that
295
\texttt{umsg} is still live when it is read:
296
 
297
\begin{verbatim}
298
/* 1.2.52 — buggy */
299
png_snprintf(umsg, sizeof umsg, msg,
300
png_ptr->chunk_name);
301
msg = umsg;
302
} /* umsg destroyed here */
303
png_warning(png_ptr, msg); /* reads dead stack! */
304
 
305
/* 1.2.53 — fixed */
306
png_snprintf(umsg, sizeof umsg, msg,
307
png_ptr->chunk_name);
308
msg = umsg;
309
png_warning(png_ptr, msg); /* called inside scope */
310
} /* umsg still alive above */
311
\end{verbatim}
312
 
313
The bug was detected by Coverity's static analyser and independently
314
rediscovered by our fuzzing campaign on version~1.2.52.
